docs.text: What is Basalo? Basalo is an international auxiliary language (IAL): a language created by a person or group of people in order to give people across the world a common, universal way of communicating with each other. These languages are often very simple—in terms of grammar, vocabulary, and even sounds—to help make the language as easy to learn as possible. Basalo, as an IAL, strives to represent three main tenets: to be simple and easy to learn, to use a vocabulary from all across the world, and to maintain cultural neutrality. Many international auxiliary languages that use words from languages worldwide will restrict their vocabulary to a specific set of languages: Lingwa de Planeta is based on 10 languages, Baseyu on 15, and Pandunia on 21, just to name a few. Basalo, however, has no restriction on what languages are represented; there are over 150 unique languages that Basalo has a word from! This gives Basalo the unique advantage of being able to represent all cultures, leveling the playing field between communities big and small. Here's a map showing just some of the languages Basalo already represents! Community and development Basalo has a dedicated community of learners and supporters in the official Discord server . In this server, people can learn and discuss Basalo, as well as suggest any changes or additions to the language. If you're interested in learning Basalo, or just want to check it out, anyone is free to join! Basalo is always growing and changing, and feedback is always appreciated.

docs.text: Guide Here's the place to learn Basalo! Don't worry if you're not very familiar with linguistics; these lessons are designed to be a smooth introduction to Basalo regardless of your skill level. 1. Sounds and spelling Learn how to read and write Basalo. Here, we'll take a look at the letters of Basalo and how to pronounce them. 2. How to make a sentence Learn how to make basic sentences. We'll learn the usage of yo , e , and la , how to form statements and questions, and introduce a few core words to play around with. 3. Making new words Learn how to create new words using compounds and kesekmolas . We'll create words for tools and occupations, make causing and becoming words, and learn the rules for compound words. 4. Incomplete, complete, and future actions Learn how to talk about when actions happen. We'll take another look at yo , introduce the particles at and sa , and learn how English tenses match to Basalo's. 5. Understanding doskamolas Learn how to use doskamolas , a collection of very useful words. Here we'll learn how to talk about "this", "every", "none", and "some", and how to ask questions like "how much?" and "who?". 6. How to make a sentence, but harder Learn how to make more complex sentences. We'll learn about modal verbs, noun phrases, and introduce prepositional verbs. 7. Names of people and places Learn how to fit names into Basalo's sound system. We'll learn some Basalo words that come from English, what sounds become which letters, and finish up by reading a few conversations. 8. Introduce yourself Make an introduction in Basalo. This'll include your name, where you're from, what you speak, and your hobbies. Congratulations on making it this far!

docs.text: table { max-width: 66%; font-size: 100%; } Lesson 1 — Sounds and spelling Basalo's alphabet consists of 19 letters; 14 consonants and 5 vowels. Basalo uses the regular English alphabet, minus the letters h , j , q , r , w , x , or z . a, b, c, d, e, f, g, i, k, l, m, n, o, p, s, t, u, v, y Sounds The unique thing about Basalo is that its sounds are able to be pronounced a variety of ways. Most are pronounced the same as in English: p, t, k — like in p ay, t ake, k ing b, d, g — like in b ay, d arn, g ame f — like in f amous m, n — like in m orning, n oon y — like in y ear, y awn a — like in f a ther i — like in t ee th or b i t u — like in t oo th or f oo t e — like in b e t o — like in oh Never pronounce vowels as an 'uh' sound, like in b u t ! A couple are pronounced sometimes like in English, but with some variations: s — like in s at, but also like th ink, th at, and z ap v — like in v ine, but also like w ine l — like in l ake, but also like r ake And the last one is pronounced much differently than in English: c — like in ch urch or j ump You might see two vowels right next to each other, or a vowel at the beginning of a word. To aid with pronunciation, it's required to add a small "stop" between each vowel or before the vowel respectively; this "stop" is like the hyphen in "uh - oh". A word like mai is pronounced like "ma-i" Stress Basalo has no contrasting stress; there's no difference between words like per mit versus per mit , like in English. Generally, any syllable can be stressed. Examples We'll look at a few words in Basalo and how to pronounce them: Basalo Meaning Pronunciation un one oon (not "uhn") salam person sah-lahm inaki dog ee-nah-kee caval horse chah-vahl, chah-wall bumi Earth boo-mee kafe coffee kah-feh yati speak yah-tee meso middle meh-soh, meh-zoh Capitalization and punctuation In Basalo, there is no capitalization needed at all. Optionally, you can use capitalization at the beginning of sentences to help with reading. Beyond that, Basalo uses most basic punctuation, like question marks, excalamtion points, periods, and commas. imut sin! — "Good to see you!" sin e mea amal, o yon! — "Meet my friend, John!" ka me kan e lel? — "Can I have it?" me kisa, ga lel yo u. — "I think that he's there." (note: the comma here is optional)

docs.text: table { max-width: 80%; font-size: 100%; } Lesson 2 — How to make a sentence Basalo sentences can be put together in a variety of ways, with a few rules: The one doing an action, or the subject , always goes first, The one experiencing an action, or the object , always has a preposition before it, And a noun that's modified by an adjective will always have la before it. For now, the object preposition will always be e , but later on we'll go over verbs with other object prepositions. Never ever forget your preposition! Statements With these rules, the basic structure is as follows: Type Example English do-er, action, object me yo yati e Basalo I'm speaking Basalo do-er, object, action le e umal yo esa he's eating an apple la noun adjective la taga imut a good day adjective la noun naya la yok a new game You'll notice that the verbs in these sentences have yo before them. This word describes an action that's unfinished or still happening, and always goes directly before the verb. However, you can get rid of this word if the do-er is a pronoun: me (yo) sin e salam. — I see a person. les e me (yo) dop ka? — Can they help me? mes e kafe (yo) esa! — We're drinking some coffee! Questions Questions are made by putting the question particle ka at the beginning or end of a sentence; sort of like a spoken question mark. le yo kan e kitap. — He has a book. ka le yo kan e kitap? — Does he have a book? le yo kan e kitap ka? — Does he have a book? Negatives In general, you can make a sentence negative by putting ma before the yo (or, as we'll see later on, the at or sa ): aman yo nalu. — The water ripples. aman ma yo nalu. — The water is not rippling. You can negate a specific word in a sentence by putting ma before it. ma inaki yo esa e mis. — The dog isn't eating the meat. inaki yo ma esa e mis. — The dog isn't eating the meat. inaki yo esa e ma mis. — The dog isn't eating the meat . Wait, how do you say "the" and "a"? You don't! Or, more precisely, there's no dedicated word for either of these. If you want to refer to one thing, you could use un , meaning "one": mama — the parent, a parent un mama — a parent, one parent And if you want to refer to some specific object, you could use lel , which means "this" or "that". We'll become more acquainted with words related to lel in Lesson 5, as it's one of the doskamolas : kin — the plant, a plant lel kin — that specific plant Remember, don't get confused with the word la ; it's just there to mark what word is a noun: la oto naya or naya la oto — a new car, the new car la umal idaman or idaman la umal — a red apple, the red apple Using lel versus le Both lel and le are very versatile words which we'll see a lot in the coming lessons. In short, le means "he" or "she", while lel can mean "this" or "that". le yo meti e lel kitap. — He's putting down that book. tes sin e le ka? — Do you guys see her? When we use lel before a noun earlier in a sentence, we can refer to that whole noun by just using lel , like so: lel salam, ka lel yo kan e mea kitap? — That guy , does he have my book? te yo sin e lel naja la yok? lel yo e aga kul. — Are you seeing that new game ? It 's super cool. Some words to start with Now that we know how to put sentences together, here's a few words you can play around with: me , te , le — I/me, you, he/she mes , tes , les — we/us, you all, they lel — this, that salam — person, man, woman mama — parent, mother, father kitap — to read; book sin — to see, look at esa — to eat, to drink; food, beverage yati — to speak, talk; speech Don't forget the important sentence-building words yo , e and la !

docs.text: table { max-width: 100%; font-size: 100%; } Work in progress! Lesson 3 — Making new words Basalo's vocabulary has many terms made up of multiple words. While sometimes these compound words are made of two full words, most of the time they're made up of one full word and one or more affixes, which in Basalo are called kesekumolas . There's quite a bit, but don't worry! We won't need to learn them all now, and you'll come to recognize them in words with time. For now, let's look at some of the most useful ones: kesekumol Meaning Examples -(a)lo tool, item naso "to write" → nasolo "pencil, pen" -(a)pi becoming, changing al "knowledge" → alapi "to learn" -(a)tel do-er, occupation fas "to create" → fasatel "creator" -(i)gi causing, result iso "equal" → isogi "to balance" -(n)ik little, small siku "ice" → sikunik "snow"
